transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-05
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO, Cobalt), Ravi Singh (Head of ML), Elena Torres (Infra Eng)

Auto-generated Summary (brief, may be imperfect):
Cobalt is evaluating Redwood dedicated reserved GPUs for production inference. Primary concerns: eviction tolerances/preemption windows, warm-pool behavior for burst traffic, VPC/KMS and audit requirements, and pricing for steady vs burst capacity. Next steps: pricing sheet, infra deep-dive and benchmark window.

Topics: reserved sizing, eviction tolerance, warm-pools, latency SLOs, KMS & SSO, fallbacks to hosted models.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — i'm Ava from Redwood, i'm the AE on your account. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Maya: Hey, good thanks. Sorry for the delay, had a back-to-back.
[00:08] Ravi: Morning all.
[00:09] Elena: Hi.
[00:11] Ava: Great. Quick intro — samir from our infra/serving team is here to walk through the ops constraints. High level agenda: we want to understand your traffic profile, what you need from reserved capacity, isolation/security controls, and your tolerance for preemption/eviction and fallback behavior. Sound ok?
[00:25] Maya: Yep. That's exactly it. We have a couple of specific concerns — we run a customer-facing NLU product, steady baseline load with periodic spikes, and regulatory requirements around data retention and key management.
[00:36] Samir: Cool. Maybe start with traffic and model footprint? Ravi, can you share typical qps and model sizes?
[00:41] Ravi: Sure. So baseline is roughly 120 qps across our ensemble of models. For heavy inference paths we use a 13B dense model and sometimes 70B for long-form generation at peak. Peak bursts hit us up to 2k qps for about 5-10 minute windows — usually promotional campaigns or scheduled releases.
[01:00] Ava: Okay that's helpful. Do you have distribution on request size? Like tokens per request?
[01:03] Ravi: Most requests are short — like 16 to 64 tokens in, 16 to 128 tokens out. The long-form generation pushes 1k+ output tokens but that's small number of requests concurrently.
[01:14] Elena: Ops constraint: we need VPC peering and KMS envelope encryption, and all request logs must be retained in our SIEM for 90 days. Also SSO with SAML — our security team won't accept anything less.
[01:27] Ava: We support VPC/private control-plane options and KMS, and can provide SOC2/ISO artefacts — we'll share the docs. The audit log retention we can discuss options for forwarding or log export.
[01:36] Maya: On preemption — what's the story with reserved nodes? If you reserve N GPUs, what's the chance of eviction and how long could preemption take to recover? We can't have 30s pauses in the middle of customer sessions.
[01:48] Samir: Good question. For Redwood Dedicated, reserved capacity means you have exclusive GPUs for your tenant in the pool. Preemption can come from hardware failures or planned maintenance; we offer warm pool and hotpool options to smooth bursts. Evictions from other tenants do not evict reserved capacity. The typical unplanned recovery time is dependent on model loading and KV cache warmup. For a cold-start reload of a 70B model that can be several minutes, maybe 3-7 minutes depending on quantization profile.
[02:18] Ravi: 3-7 minutes is pretty long for a chat flow. Can you do incremental warm starts or keep a standby preloaded?
[02:23] Samir: Yes — hotpool (we sometimes call it warm-pool) can keep preloaded model artifacts and KV caches ready. It costs more, but can reduce tail recovery to sub-10s for smaller models and sub-60s for larger ones if the hotpool is sized correctly. There's also our prefix/KV caching which helps for conversational sessions so you don't need a full reload for every user context.
[02:41] Elena: And the hotpool eviction policy — if we pay for X hotpool slots, are those guaranteed? Or are they charged as soft credits?
[02:49] Ava: Reserved GPUs are firm; hotpool slots are part of the reserved plan — you can reserve warm-pool capacity as part of your commit. We can add guardrails for prewarming thresholds and max eviction probability in the SLA.
[02:58] Maya: Another question: fallback. If our reserved pool is saturated because of an unexpected surge, can Redwood route to hosted variants or smaller quantized models to maintain latency?
[03:07] Samir: Yes. Smart routing policies can failover to compatible model variants in lower tiers — e.g., 70B -> 13B quantized -> hosted 13B. You can configure per-route fallbacks and percent-based rollouts. That is commonly used to trade quality for latency during storming events.
[03:22] Ravi: If we do that, how do we validate quality regressions? We need to know customer-visible deltas.
[03:27] Ava: We recommend shipping a small prompt set / eval harness. We can run correlated A/B checks during the failover window or provide simulated fallbacks in a staging benchmark so you can measure deviations. We'll include guidance in the SOW.
[03:36] Elena: Ok, ops question again — networking. We will be on an isolated VPC with private endpoints. How do we handle egress logging? We need the ability to export raw request metadata to our Splunk.
[03:46] Samir: We can enable log forwarding via our private collector — logs can be pushed to your S3 or syslog endpoint, or delivered via an agent inside the VPC. Sensitive payloads can be redacted; we also support customer-managed key rotation for stored artifacts.
[03:58] Maya: Pricing: how's burst billing modeled? Is it a per-minute overage or a credit system? We want predictability but flexible headroom.
[04:05] Ava: For dedicated customers we offer reserved commit with two common patterns: steady-reserve (monthly committed GPUs with discounted per-token usage) plus burst credits (prepaid or pay-as-you-go). Typically customers buy a base reservation for baseline and then either buy burst credits or allow autoscale with overage billing at a different rate. We can show a comparison in a pricing sheet.
[04:24] Ravi: Do you support preemptible cheaper nodes for background or batch jobs? We could run batch reranks on cheap preemptible capacity.
[04:30] Samir: Yes, you can have a hybrid — reserved for critical low-latency paths and spot/preemptible pools for batch processing. Our routing and orchestration can move workloads between them, and you can pin models to specific tiers.
[04:39] Elena: SLA: we need SLOs for 99th percentile latency and clear definitions for when failover is triggered. Can we get custom SLAs?
[04:46] Ava: Enterprise contracts can include custom SLAs. We'll capture your 99th P99 latency targets and craft the SLA. Typical P99 targets we've seen set between 400-1200 ms depending on the model and sequence length. What are you targeting?
[04:59] Maya: For our realtime flows we need P95 < 300ms and P99 < 900ms on the 13B paths; for 70B we accept higher, but ideally P99 < 2.5s.
[05:10] Samir: Achievable with a combination of reserved GPUs and hotpool sizing; we'll need to tune batch sizes and quantization. Also sequence length distribution matters — shorter sequences are much cheaper on latency.
[05:20] Ravi: On quantization—what options do you have? 4-bit, 8-bit? Any issues with quality loss for our models?
[05:26] Samir: We support INT8 and custom 4-bit quant profiles depending on the model and customer acceptance. There is a quality tradeoff; for some models 4-bit is still high quality for embeddings and classification but may degrade long-form generation. We include quantization recommendations in Redwood Optimize.
[05:39] Elena: Security: KMS — can we bring our own key (BYOK) and do HSM-backed wrapping?
[05:44] Ava: Yes, BYOK and HSM support are available for Private deployments. For Hosted, we offer KMS integration with customer-managed keys in many regions — we can send the integration guide.
[05:53] Maya: One more about logs: we need immutable audit logs for compliance. Can you provide an append-only audit trail with tamper evidence?
[06:00] Samir: We can provide signed audit logs and forward them to your archival bucket under your control. For Private deployments you can enable on-prem audit chains as well.
[06:08] Ravi: Let's talk numbers — what's the recommended reserved capacity for our profile? 120 qps baseline + 2k spikes, mixed models.
[06:16] Samir: We'll ballpark. For 13B models, one A100-like GPU (assuming optimized runtime and quantized) can handle roughly X concurrent short requests — in our field data that's about 250-400 qps depending on batching and request size. For 70B models, concurrency is much lower. Given your baseline, a conservative commit might be 4-6 GPUs for baseline (13B paths) with 2 warm-pool preloads of 70B to cover the occasional long-form jobs, plus burst credits to ramp when you hit 2k qps. But this is rough — we'd like to run an actual capacity sizing workshop.
[06:48] Maya: Sounds reasonable as a starting point. We also need to understand failure modes — if the hotpool depletes during a sustained 20-minute spike, what's the fallback timeline and how do we throttle?
[06:58] Samir: We have request-level shaping and tenant soft-quota to slow new sessions once a hotpool is exhausted. Fallback routing can progressively route new requests to quantized variants. Existing sessions with KV context might experience higher latency until the model reloads. We'll provide a failure case matrix in the deep dive.
[07:14] Ava: Quick interruption — i want to capture three things as next follow-ups: 1) pricing sheet with burst+warmpool options, 2) a technical deep-dive/benchmark with Samir + Elena, and 3) SOC2 and KMS docs. We'll also propose a 48-hour benchmark window.
[07:28] Maya: Agree. Also, we want a small POC that exercises the failover path so we can validate user-visible regression.
[07:34] Ravi: On the POC — we'll provide a representative workload and prompts. We need measurement around user latency and accuracy delta.
[07:41] Samir: Good. We'll build a benchmark harness that can replay your traffic and simulate spikes; we'll include A/B comparison tooling.
[07:49] Elena: About network egress — do we get ability to tag request IDs and correlate logs?
[07:54] Samir: Yes, request IDs can be propagated and correlated with logs and traces. We can also include RT metrics in the console.
[07:59] Maya: Any compliance gaps vs our infosec checklist we should know?
[08:03] Ava: Not that i can think of — most is covered by our enterprise package; specifics like data residency, special audit controls we'll check and call out in the SOC2 docs.
[08:12] Ravi: Competitor question — we evaluated OtherCloudAI and SelfHostOps internally. OtherCloudAI had lower latency on their 13B hosted tier but lacked private KMS integration; SelfHostOps required a bigger engineering lift. How do you position yourselves?
[08:24] Ava: We position as production-first with flexible deployment modes: hosted for quick start, dedicated for predictable throughput, and private for regulated workloads. Our selling point is the unified API and strong ops controls. We try to be the middle ground — less lift than self-hosting, more control than simple hosted providers.
[08:40] Maya: That matches what we're looking for. One more granular question: can you stitch compute tiers so individual routes have throttles and fallbacks? E.g., search route pinned to reserved GPUs, and long-form route allowed to overflow to hosted.
[08:52] Samir: Absolutely. Per-route policies are the standard — you can set route-level SLOs, fallback order, and max-percent failover.
[08:59] Ava: We're approaching 40 minutes in the call — maybe wrap with concrete next steps and owners.
[09:05] Maya: Sure.
[09:06] Ava: So action items: i'll send pricing and a short feature matrix (Ava). Samir will schedule the technical deep-dive and draft the benchmark plan (Samir). Elena to share traffic profiles and security checklist items (Elena). We'll target the deep dive week of Dec 8–12 — does Dec 11 work?
[09:23] Elena: Dec 11 is fine for me.
[09:25] Ravi: Works.
[09:26] Maya: Works on our side.
[09:27] Ava: Great. Anything else?
[09:29] Ravi: One small note — can we get an indicative cost for a configuration like the 4-6 GPU baseline + 2 warmpool slots and 10% burst credits? Even a ballpark helps our procurement.
[09:40] Ava: We'll include a ballpark in the pricing sheet.
[09:43] Maya: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[09:45] Ava: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the materials, and Samir will send a calendar invite for the deep dive.
[09:50] [meeting ends]
